etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English recorde, borrowed from Old French record, from recorder. See record (verb).

definitions.definition: An item of information put into a temporary or permanent physical medium.

quote.citation: 2012 March-April, John T. Jost, “Social Justice: Is It in Our Nature (and Our Future)?”, in American Scientist‎[1], volume 100, number 2, archived from the original on 13 February 2012, page 162:
quote.text: He draws eclectically on studies of baboons, descriptive anthropological accounts of hunter-gatherer societies and, in a few cases, the fossil record.

definitions.definition: Any instance of a physical medium on which information was put for the purpose of preserving it and making it available for future reference.
Ellipsis of phonograph record: a disc, usually made from vinyl, on which sound is recorded and may be replayed on a phonograph.

quote.text: He's the record doctor / Tell him your woes / He'll reach in his bag / And he'll give you a dose

definitions.definition: (computing) A set of data relating to a single individual or item.
(programming) A data structure similar to a struct, in some programming languages such as C# and Java based on classes and designed for storing immutable data.

quote.citation: 1989, Elliot B. Koffman, Pascal: Problem Solving and Program Design, Addison-Wesley, →ISBN, page 406:
quote.text: This chapter examines another data structure, the record (available in Pascal but not in all other high-level languages). Records make it easier to organize and represent information in Pascal, a major reason for the popularity of the Pascal […]

quote.citation: 2020, Ian F. Darwin, Java Cookbook, O'Reilly Media, →ISBN, page 232:
quote.text: The new record type provides another solution. A record is a class-like construct for data classes, a restricted form of class like enums and annotations.

quote.citation: 2021, Joseph Albahari, C# 9.0 in a Nutshell, O'Reilly Media, →ISBN, page 210:
quote.text: A record is a special kind of class that's designed to work well with immutable (readonly) data.

definitions.definition: The most extreme known value of some variable, particularly that of an achievement in competitive events.

quote.citation: 2023 April 5, “Network News: Conservatives accused of "rewarding Avanti's failure"”, in RAIL, number 980, page 6:
quote.text: "Avanti has literally broken records over the last six months for delays and cancellations, and the Conservatives' answer is to reward failure with millions more in taxpayer cash," said Labour Shadow Transport Secretary Louise Haigh.

definitions.definition: (attributive) Enough to break previous records and set a new one; world-class; historic.

quote.citation: 1952, C. S. Lewis, The Voyage of the Dawn Treader:
quote.text: "But it's far worse for me," said Edmund, "because you'll at least have a room of your own and I shall have to share a bedroom with that record stinker, Eustace."

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English recorden (“to repeat, to report”), borrowed from Old French recorder (“to get by heart”), from Latin recordārī (“remember, call to mind”), from re- (“back, again”) + cor (“heart; mind”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To make a record of information.

quote.citation: 2012 September 7, Phil McNulty, “Moldova 0-5 England”, in BBC Sport‎[2]:
quote.text: The display and result must be placed in the context that was it was against a side that looked every bit their Fifa world ranking of 141 - but England completed the job with efficiency to record their biggest away win in 19 years.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To make an audio or video recording of.

quote.citation: 2014 June 29, Adam Sherwin, “UK cinemas ban Google glasses over piracy risk”, in The Independent‎[3]:
quote.text: However, the ability to record people without their knowledge, with the stroke of a finger over the spectacle frame or a voice command, has prompted privacy concerns.

definitions.definition: (transitive, law) To give legal status to by making an official public record.
(intransitive) To fix in a medium, usually in a tangible medium.
(intransitive) To make an audio, video, or multimedia recording.
(transitive, intransitive, obsolete) To repeat; to practice.
(transitive, intransitive, obsolete) To sing or repeat a tune.

quote.citation: 1595, George Peele, The Old Wives’ Tale, The Malone Society Reprints, 1908, lines 741-742,[4]
quote.text:
Come Berecynthia, let vs in likewise,
And heare the Nightingale record hir notes.

quote.citation: 1600, Torquato Tasso, translated by Edward Fairfax, Godfrey of Bulloigne, or The Recouerie of Ierusalem‎[5], London: I. Iaggard and M. Lownes, Book 2, p. 39:
quote.text: They long’d to see the day, to heare the larkeRecord her hymnes and chant her carols blest,

quote.citation: c. 1607–1608, William Shakeſpeare, The Late, And much admired Play, Called Pericles, Prince of Tyre. […], London: Imprinted at London for Henry Goſſon,  […], published 1609, →OCLC, [Act IV, Prologue]:
quote.text: […]  to the luteShe sung, and made the night-bird mute,That still records with moan;

quote.citation: 1616, William Browne, Britannia’s Pastorals‎[6], London: John Haviland, published 1625, Book 2, Song 4, p. 129:
quote.text: […]  the Nymph did earnestly contestWhether the Birds or she recorded best  […]

quote.citation: 1655, Thomas Fuller, “Section 3”, in The Church-history of Britain; […], London:  […]  Iohn Williams […], →OCLC, (please specify |book=I to XI), page 204:
